results.summary_before: This is a Verilog implementation of the classic Space Invaders game. The player controls a ship using three input buttons to move left, move right, and shoot, with the game state output on eight pins. It is intended to be played using the TinyTapeout Commander app, which maps keyboard inputs to the ASIC pins, and tested with the TinyTapeout VGA Playground. No external hardware is required beyond the standard TinyTapeout setup, and no silicon test results are mentioned.

results.summary_before: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

results.summary_before: Wirecube is a demo for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition that displays a rotating wireframe cube on a VGA screen. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and operates at a clock frequency of 50.35 MHz. Inputs allow toggling background and cube colors, as well as speed. The documentation is sparse and will be updated after the competition, but the design is functional as a visual demo.

results.summary_before: This design displays symbols on a 7-segment LED display based on an 8-bit input binary word, and it outputs the letter n only when the input equals 0b00010101. It is tested by trying different input words and verifying that outputs 0, 1, 2, 4, and 5 are high only for that specific input. External hardware includes eight input switches and a 7-segment LED display. The project is a simple Wokwi exercise in binary pattern detection and seven-segment output, with clear but limited documentation.

results.summary_before: ShadyPong is a Pong game implementation in SystemVerilog that outputs VGA signals on uo[0] to uo[7], matching the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. Four inputs control player up and down movements, a fifth forces a fallback ball speed, and the bidirectional pins expose ball and player speed values. It runs at 25.175 MHz and requires a TinyVGA PMOD or an iCEsugar VGA PMOD with flying wires. The documentation is very sparse, with the how-it-works and how-to-test sections giving no real detail, so behaviour beyond the pinout is largely inferred.
